chunks: My father, may Allah grant him mercy, said: We were told by Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Musa ibn Umar, from Musa ibn Bakr, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

An Arabian came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his Family) and said to him: Are you not the best of us in terms of father and mother, the most generous among us in terms of progeny, and our leader during the Jahiliyyah and Islam? Then the Prophet (peace be upon him and his Family) was angered and said: O Arabian, how many covers are before your tongue? He said: Two: two lips and teeth. Then the Prophet (peace be upon him and his Family) said: So, what was in either of these two that repels the wandering of this tongue of yours? Verily, none has been given anything in this life of his that is more harmful to him in his afterlife than the unrestraint of his tongue! O Ali, stand up and cut his tongue! Then the people assumed that he will cut his tongue, but (instead) he gave him dirhams.
ai.seo_question: What is the meaning behind the Prophet's command to Ali to 'cut the tongue' of the boastful Arabian?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Mani al-Akhbar* highlights the Prophet’s acute awareness of the tongue’s potential for both harm and grace, using the physical limitations of lips and teeth as a metaphor for unchecked speech. While the command to Ali to 'cut his tongue' initially suggests a literal physical punishment, the narrative clarifies it as a rhetorical device to emphasize the severity of loquacity, ultimately resolved by Ali’s wisdom in granting a monetary gift rather than inflicting physical harm. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the practical application of prophetic authority and the balance between justice and mercy in dealing with tribal arrogance.
